summary: 15 concise trial-paper-only hypotheses distilled from the ResearchAgent run for ist3, grouped by the characteristic each names.

mechanisms.description: Higher baseline age may reduce the net benefit of alteplase because age‑related cerebral frailty and comorbidity increase susceptibility to symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage and limit potential for functional recovery after reperfusion.

Longer onset-to-treatment time likely attenuates alteplase benefit because progressive infarct core growth reduces salvageable tissue and raises the probability of hemorrhagic conversion following fibrinolysis.

Very severe baseline NIHSS may diminish proportional benefit from alteplase because extensive early ischemia leaves less recoverable brain and increases risk of hemorrhagic transformation after thrombolysis.

Markedly elevated systolic blood pressure at presentation may increase harm from alteplase by promoting blood–brain barrier disruption and hematoma expansion, thereby raising symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage risk.

Higher admission blood glucose may reduce alteplase efficacy and increase bleeding complications because hyperglycemia aggravates ischemic injury and contributes to blood–brain barrier breakdown that predisposes to hemorrhage.

Presence of atrial fibrillation may modify treatment effect because cardioembolic strokes often carry larger clot burden that can confer greater potential benefit from reperfusion but also associate with larger infarcts and higher hemorrhagic conversion risk after thrombolysis.

Higher prestroke mRS likely lowers the absolute benefit of alteplase because limited baseline functional reserve reduces the chance of achieving independence despite reperfusion and magnifies the clinical impact of symptomatic hemorrhage.

Concurrent antiplatelet therapy at baseline may shift the balance toward harm with alteplase by impairing primary hemostasis and increasing the likelihood and severity of intracranial bleeding after fibrinolysis.

Therapeutic anticoagulant use at baseline is likely to reduce alteplase safety because systemic anticoagulation potentiates bleeding risk when fibrinolysis is administered, increasing the chance of symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage.

Low ASPECTS (extensive early ischemic change) on baseline CT likely diminishes alteplase benefit because a large established infarct core predicts poor functional recovery and greater susceptibility to hemorrhagic transformation after thrombolysis.

Presence of a large‑vessel occlusion may increase absolute benefit from alteplase through greater opportunity for reperfusion and downstream tissue salvage, while persistent proximal occlusion or large territory risk can also amplify hemorrhagic complications.

Poor collateral circulation on baseline angiography likely reduces alteplase benefit because insufficient collateral flow accelerates core expansion, limiting salvageable tissue and increasing the risk of hemorrhagic conversion once reperfusion occurs.
Low platelet count at baseline may amplify harm from alteplase by impairing primary hemostasis and increasing both the likelihood and severity of intracranial bleeding after fibrinolytic therapy.

Severely reduced eGFR may worsen the hemorrhagic risk profile of alteplase because uremic platelet dysfunction and vascular fragility predispose to bleeding and may blunt post‑reperfusion neurological recovery.

Extremes of body mass index may modify alteplase effect because low BMI can increase effective drug exposure and bleeding risk while obesity‑related comorbidity and altered physiological reserve can reduce functional gains from reperfusion.
